title: Farming under pressure: fisheries, disease, water and SFI turmoil
label: 27 October 2026 · The future of farming
summary: Minster Stephen Morgan and DEFRA directors gave evidence on fisheries negotiations, disease outbreaks and animal welfare, drought and water resilience, and major problems with the Sustainable Farming Incentive (SFI). Officials stressed following science in fisheries talks, work to support farmers through bluetongue and TB outbreaks, and measures to boost drought resilience; they admitted SFI window 2 was oversubscribed, that first-come first-served caused distress, and promised to scrap that approach while explaining limited budgets and reallocation across ELMs.

glossary.definition: Total Allowable Catch: the limit set for how much of a fish stock can be caught in a year.
International Council for the Exploration of the Sea: independent scientists who advise on fish stock health.
Marine Management Organisation: the UK regulator that engages with the fishing industry.
Sustainable Farming Incentive: a DEFRA scheme that pays farmers for actions that deliver public environmental benefits.
Environmental Land Management schemes: the set of public schemes (including SFI, higher tier, landscape recovery) that pay for environmental outcomes on farms.
Animal and Plant Health Agency: DEFRA's agency responsible for animal disease testing and control.
The Pirbright Institute: a UK research centre working on animal infectious diseases.
Sanitary and Phytosanitary agreement: trade rules on food safety and animal/plant health between countries.
National Farmers' Union: the main farming membership organisation in England and Wales.
Rural Payments Agency: DEFRA's agency that runs farm payments and manages scheme applications.
Site of Special Scientific Interest: a legally protected area for wildlife or geology.
Higher Level Stewardship: an older agri-environment agreement due to expire and transition into new schemes.
An ELMs scheme funding long-term, large-scale environmental projects across multiple landowners.
An agri-environment scheme for targeted land management actions, part of the ELMs suite.
Energy Intensive Industry compensation: support for businesses facing high energy costs, tied to industrial classifications.

chapters.title: Fisheries: who negotiates and who decides?
chapters.takeaway: DEFRA officials lead negotiations using scientific advice; ministers set priorities but made no firm promise on a fisheries strategy or on changing access deals with Norway.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Who leads the year-end fisheries negotiations for the UK?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: DEFRA officials lead the detailed talks; I set the negotiation principles and engage with industry and counterparts as needed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Will you produce a UK fishing strategy in the next 12 months?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: I agree there is no clear strategy at the moment. I'm keen to work with officials and the sector to set a long-term vision, but I didn't commit to a 12-month deadline today.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: ICES advised a zero TAC for Northern Shelf cod. That treats three biological sub-stocks as one; do you accept that approach?

turns.speaker: Gareth Baynham-Hughes
turns.text: We start from the science. ICES set up a 'tiger team' to study sub-stock questions and gave scenarios for negotiations. A zero TAC is very difficult because of bycatch and impacts on other fisheries; negotiations must reflect the science.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Norway caught much more whitefish in UK waters than we did in theirs last year. Will the UK seek a fairer balance?

turns.speaker: Gareth Baynham-Hughes
turns.text: Some parts of the fleet benefit from reciprocal access and others feel disadvantaged. We will press for the best UK position with Norway, taking industry inputs into account.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Fishermen say large foreign trawlers are taking small saithe, hurting Shetland. Is that acceptable?

turns.speaker: Gareth Baynham-Hughes
turns.text: We know catch composition and local pressures matter; spatial or targeted closures are among the measures we can consider. These issues are on the table for negotiation.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Fuel costs are forcing boats to stop fishing. Other EU states are giving state aid. Will the UK help?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: We recognise fishermen's pressures. There is existing fuel tax support and we're reviewing options, including whether to reallocate existing funds, but there's no live UK equivalent to those EU aids yet.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Will any SPS deal with the EU affect UK fisheries management?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: I can't discuss negotiation detail here, but protecting British interests and our sovereign fishing policy remains vital.

chapters.title: Animal disease and welfare: bluetongue, TB and stunning
chapters.takeaway: DEFRA supported vaccine supply and testing for bluetongue, will publish the TB strategy next stage before Christmas, and opened a consultation on pig stunning despite industry concerns about the evidence base.

turns.speaker: Sarah Bool
turns.text: Bluetongue caused thousands of cases this year and big disposal costs. What support will you give affected farmers?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: We worked with industry to ensure vaccine supply, improved testing, helped fallen stock processes, and published heat maps. We're doing lessons learned and monitoring the situation closely.

turns.speaker: Sarah Bool
turns.text: Some countries subsidise bluetongue vaccines. Will the UK do the same?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: At present we are not subsidising vaccines or making them mandatory; uptake decisions remain between farmers and vets. We emphasise clear communication to encourage vaccination.

turns.speaker: Sarah Dyke
turns.text: On TB: when will you respond to the June control strategy and improve testing accuracy?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: We have adopted the strategy and will publish the next stage before Christmas. We are developing cattle and badger vaccines, expanding testing, and establishing an industry-government board to drive delivery.

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: Officials are exploring all tools, including wider use of interferon-gamma testing and private blood tests to spot infection earlier and reduce unnecessary culling.

turns.speaker: Josh Newbury
turns.text: You opened a consultation about phasing out CO2 stunning for pigs in favour of argon or electric systems, but the Animal Welfare Committee notes worrying welfare signals. Is the evidence strong enough?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: The consultation is intended to gather industry evidence before Ministers decide. I encourage stakeholders to respond; I will convene a summit to discuss pig sector pressures and implementation risks.

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: The consultation follows the Animal Welfare Committee's recommendation; it's the step to collect more evidence from industry about welfare, practicality and cost.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The pig sector fears a Christmas backlog of animals if abattoirs can't convert quickly. Will your summit address this immediate welfare risk?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: Yes. I want to work with processors and industry to identify short-term solutions and longer-term market forecasting to avoid backlogs that create welfare issues.

chapters.title: Water, drought and wildfires: reservoirs and licences
chapters.takeaway: DEFRA increased funding for on-farm water measures and is working across government to speed up licences and planning, but system and planning barriers remain.

turns.speaker: Terry Jermy
turns.text: Farmers need water licences and planning changes fast. When will getting abstraction licences and building reservoirs become easier?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: We have a £15m water management grant and set milestones through the farming and food partnership board with MHCLG and the Environment Agency to speed up planning and abstraction processes.

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: We're looking at smart abstraction pilots and automatic river monitoring to cut licence complexity and at where finance can speed reservoir construction; results should start showing next year.

turns.speaker: Helena Dollimore
turns.text: You reallocated £50m into SFI for drought resilience. Was that ring-fenced for drought measures?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: We made £50m available; details of applications will be published next month.

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: We didn't ring-fence the £50m inside SFI because system changes would have delayed opening; we prioritised getting help out quickly but will consider tighter ring-fencing next year.

turns.speaker: Helena Dollimore
turns.text: Farmers helped fight wildfires with firebreaks. Will DEFRA support farmers in preparedness and give local resilience forums better links to landowners?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: We praised farmers' actions at the wildfire summit and are adding wildfire-focused actions into environmental schemes and improving local preparedness through local resilience forums.

chapters.title: SFI window 2: oversubscription and fallout
chapters.takeaway: SFI window 2 closed within hours, leaving many farmers without agreements; DEFRA accepts the process failed in practice, will scrap first-come, first-served, and is reviewing budgets and exceptional cases.

turns.speaker: Sarah Bool
turns.text: How many expiring agreements did you expect, how many applied in window 2, and what budget covered it?

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: We had in excess of 20,000 expiring agreements. Window 2 received about 12,200 applications. The budget was increased from about £180m to around £253m after extra allocations, but demand still outstripped supply.

turns.speaker: Sarah Bool
turns.text: So thousands who expected to renew missed out. Why keep first-come, first-served knowing demand was high?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: I have already said we will move away from first-come, first-served. The scheme design was set before my appointment but I accept the distress caused and will learn lessons.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The NFU estimates expiring agreements were worth £520m but SFI windows total £310m—a £210m gap. Where does that money go?

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: There isn't 'missing' money. The wider farming budget is finite; some historic agreements move into higher tier or landscape recovery and the overall spending envelope is allocated across the ELMs suite.

turns.speaker: Sarah Bool
turns.text: DEFRA added an exceptions process for people who had technical problems. How many will be accepted and what will it cost?

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: RPA is reviewing two groups—those needing digital help and those reporting system issues—and will contact applicants individually. Our estimate is the cost is under £5m, depending on outcomes.

turns.speaker: Josh Newbury
turns.text: SFI is public money for public goods, unlike Basic Payment. Will you track how many farms end up with no ELM revenue by 2027?

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: We have 84,000 live ELM revenue agreements now. The exact number without revenue by 2027 depends on next year's scheme design; we will model and publish data as plans solidify.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Farmers feel confidence in DEFRA's delivery has been damaged. How will you rebuild trust?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: By co-designing the scheme with industry and parliamentarians, publishing clearer proposals early, scrapping first-come, first-served and fixing RPA/technical issues so people can plan.

chapters.title: Higher tier, landscape recovery and uplands
chapters.takeaway: Higher tier and landscape recovery are delivering but are complex; officials will simplify administration, tackle common-land software issues, and handle upland HLS expiries case by case.

turns.speaker: Josh Newbury
turns.text: Is countryside stewardship higher tier and landscape recovery delivering value for money and access for smaller farms?

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: We're opening higher tier with new single-action agreements and an expression-of-interest process; since launching we've approved 751 agreements worth £31.8m. Landscape recovery is novel and complex—56 projects in development, three in implementation—so we're advising Ministers how to speed delivery.

turns.speaker: Josh Newbury
turns.text: Projects like Greater Sedgemoor are ready to implement but waiting. Can DEFRA prioritise getting those on the ground?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: Yes. I'll review their status and press officials to move ready projects to implementation and address the two-year withdrawal concern that discourages farmers from joining.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: What about uplands like Dartmoor and HLS expiries? Farmers fear cliff-edge losses and blanket de-stocking.

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: We are taking a cohort-by-cohort approach driven by SSSI condition. Natural England advises on site condition; transitions will vary by area rather than a single national rule.

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: I want place-based, community-led work in uplands—Hilary Cottam's efforts are an example—and I will press for tailored solutions rather than blunt reductions.

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: Common land eligibility is a legacy issue in the systems. The RPA is piloting access to higher tier on common land; SFI currently excludes it but we're working to fix that.

chapters.title: Abattoirs, markets and sector growth plans
chapters.takeaway: DEFRA accepts local abattoir closures are a problem, wants to ease regulation, produce sector growth plans (horticulture, poultry) and explore private finance for nature markets, but funding is limited.

turns.speaker: Helena Dollimore
turns.text: Local abattoirs are disappearing. Will DEFRA treat them as vital infrastructure and fund or support them?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: We work with an abattoir working group and task-and-finish groups to reduce regulatory burdens and examine what support might help; the Smaller Abattoir Fund closed but we are considering options.

turns.speaker: Ben Goldsborough
turns.text: Protected horticulture needs SIC codes to access EII support for energy. Will you press other Departments to fix that so growers can compete?

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: Horticulture is a priority in our sector growth plans. The partnership board has cross-Government membership; if a SIC code change is warranted it will be raised and pursued.

turns.speaker: Ben Goldsborough
turns.text: DEFRA's roadmap expects private nature markets to help fund environmental land management—how will you make those markets work for upland and smaller farms?

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: We published 'Growing Places' and set up a working group to identify where private finance works and remove barriers. It's patchy now; we'll try to scale successful models and protect public funding where private finance can't operate.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Finally, there's concern about optics: DEFRA funding part of the Rothbury Estate purchase while many farmers missed SFI offers. How do you respond?

turns.speaker: Mike Rowe
turns.text: That funding was outside the farming budget and tied to international biodiversity commitments. We must balance international obligations with domestic priorities and ensure tenant impacts are managed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. We'll follow up on outstanding issues—wool market, milking goats, and detailed SFI data—by correspondence.

turns.speaker: Stephen Morgan
turns.text: Thank you. We will provide further detail and work with the Committee while we implement lessons and plans for the future.
